entries.original: Doubling one factor and halving the other leaves the product unchanged; a factor next to a multiple of ten is that multiple minus (or plus) one group. / Keep doubling one factor and halving the other until one of them is a ten, a hundred or another easy number. Or round a factor to the nearest multiple of ten, multiply, then take away (or add) the extra group.
text: Doubling one factor and halving the other leaves the product unchanged. If a factor is one less (or one more) than a multiple of ten, multiply by that multiple of ten and take away (or add) one group of the other factor: 19 × 4 = 20 × 4 − 4.

Keep doubling one factor and halving the other until one of them is a ten, a hundred or another easy number. Or round a factor to the nearest multiple of ten, multiply, then take away (or add) the extra group.
entries.problem: 'a factor next to a multiple of ten is that multiple minus (or plus) one group' is garbled.

entries.original: Draw 8 rows of 7 dots. Count 5 rows (35) and 3 more rows (21).
text: Draw 8 rows of 7 dots. Count 5 rows (35) and 3 more rows (21).
entries.problem: It counts 35 and 21 but never adds them to reach 7 × 8 = 56.

entries.original: In a two-digit number the tens digit matters most: 71 is more than 17 because 7 tens is more than 1 ten. / For the greatest, put the biggest digit in the tens place and the next biggest in the ones. For the smallest, put the smallest digit that is not 0 in the tens place.
text: In a two-digit number the tens digit matters most: 71 is more than 17 because 7 tens is more than 1 ten.

For the greatest, put the biggest digit in the tens place and the next biggest in the ones. For the smallest, put the smallest digit that is not 0 in the tens place and the smallest digit left (0 if you have it) in the ones.
entries.problem: The rule for the smallest number says what goes in the tens place but not what goes in the ones place.

entries.original: Twin primes are pairs of prime numbers that are 2 apart, such as 11 and 13. Both numbers must be prime, and the gap must be exactly 2. / For each pair, first check the gap is 2. Then test each number: try dividing by 2, 3, 5 and 7. If neither number divides, the pair are twin primes.
text: Twin primes are pairs of prime numbers that are 2 apart, such as 11 and 13. Both numbers must be prime, and the gap must be exactly 2.

For each pair, first check the gap is 2. Then test each number (up to 100) by dividing by 2, 3, 5 and 7. If none of these divides either number exactly (other than the number itself), the pair are twin primes.
entries.problem: 'If neither number divides' is garbled, and testing 2, 3, 5, 7 only works below 121 and when the number is not itself one of them.

entries.original: Write the numbers in a grid. Cross out 1. / Keep 2 and cross out every other multiple of 2; keep 3 and cross out its multiples; do the same for 5 and 7. The numbers left are prime.
text: Write the numbers in a grid. Cross out 1.
Keep 2 and cross out all the other multiples of 2; keep 3 and cross out its other multiples; do the same for 5 and 7. The numbers left are prime.
entries.problem: 'Cross out every other multiple of 2' can be read as crossing out alternate multiples.

entries.original: a^(p/q) is the q-th root of a, raised to the power p: (ᵠ√a)ᵖ = ᵠ√(aᵖ). A negative power gives the reciprocal. / Take the root first (the denominator), then the power (the numerator); for a negative power, take the reciprocal at the end.
text: a^(p/q) is the q-th root of a, raised to the power p: (q-th root of a)ᵖ = q-th root of (aᵖ). A negative power gives the reciprocal.
Take the root first (the denominator), then the power (the numerator); for a negative power, take the reciprocal at the end.
entries.problem: Writes the q-th root as 'ᵠ√' (a superscript phi), which is not q and confuses the notation.

entries.original: Ratios compare by multiplication. a : b and c : d are equivalent when a/b = c/d; the one with the larger fraction is the greater ratio. / Cross-multiply: compare a × d with b × c. Equal products mean equivalent ratios; otherwise the larger product shows the greater ratio. Or write both with the same second term.
text: Ratios compare by multiplication. a : b and c : d are equivalent when a/b = c/d; the one with the larger fraction is the greater ratio.
Cross-multiply: compare a × d with b × c. Equal products mean equivalent ratios; if a × d is larger, a : b is greater; if b × c is larger, c : d is greater. Or write both with the same second term.
entries.problem: 'The larger product shows the greater ratio' does not say which product belongs to which ratio.

entries.original: Between two integers the number line can be cut into q equal parts; each part is 1/q. A rational number halfway between x and y is their average. / Start at the named end and move s parts of 1/q (right adds, left subtracts). For halfway, add the two numbers and divide by 2.
text: Between two integers the number line can be cut into q equal parts; each part is 1/q. A rational number halfway between x and y is their average.

Start at the number the question names and move the given number of parts, each 1/q long (right adds, left subtracts): for example, starting at 2 and moving 3 parts of 1/4 to the right gives 2 3/4. For halfway, add the two numbers and divide by 2.
entries.problem: Uses q, s and 'the named end' without saying what they are.

entries.original: So we look for the whole number whose square is 2809.
text: √2809 is the whole number that, multiplied by itself, makes 2809.
50 × 50 = 2500 and 60 × 60 = 3600, so the root is between 50 and 60. 2809 ends in 9, so the root ends in 3 or 7.
entries.problem: Promises a step-by-step method but is a single fragment starting with 'So', with no steps or answer.

entries.original: Bayes' theorem turns the question round: P(Bag I | red) = P(Bag I and red) / P(red), and P(red) adds up the red branches of both bags (total probability). / Draw a tree: first the bag (with the die's probabilities), then the colour. Multiply along each red branch; divide the Bag I red branch by the sum of both red branches.
text: Bayes' theorem turns the question round: P(Bag I | red) = P(Bag I and red)
P(red), and P(red) adds up the red branches of both bags (total probability).

Draw a tree: first the bag (with the probability of choosing each bag, for example from a die throw), then the colour. Multiply along each red branch; divide the Bag I red branch by the sum of both red branches.
entries.problem: Mentions 'the die's probabilities' although no die has been described.

entries.original: The bag has 9 + 7 + 3 = 19 balls of the same size, so each of the 19 balls is equally likely to be taken. / The event "blue" happens for 7 of them, so its probability is 7 out of 19.
text: A bag has 9 red, 7 blue and 3 green balls of the same size: 9 + 7 + 3 = 19 balls, so each of the 19 balls is equally likely to be taken.
The event "blue" happens for 7 of them, so its probability is 7 out of 19, 7/19.
entries.problem: It refers to 9 + 7 + 3 balls and the event 'blue' without saying what is in the bag or which number is blue.

entries.original: Imagine numbering the balls 1 to 18. Each number is as likely as any other. / 8 of the 18 numbers are on red balls, so the probability is 8 out of 18.
text: A bag has 8 red, 7 blue and 3 green balls. Imagine numbering the 18 balls 1 to 18. Each number is as likely as any other.
8 of the 18 numbers are on red balls, so the probability of red is 8 out of 18, 8/18 = 4/9.
entries.problem: It talks of 18 balls with 8 red without describing the bag.

entries.original: The event "green" happens for 6 of them, so its probability is 6 out of 18.
text: A bag has 3 red, 9 blue and 6 green balls of the same size: 3 + 9 + 6 = 18 balls, each equally likely to be taken.
The event "green" happens for 6 of them, so its probability is 6 out of 18, 6/18 = 1/3.
entries.problem: 'Step by step' gives one sentence about 'them' without saying what the bag holds; the total 18 and the 6 green balls appear from nowhere.

entries.original: A question: “A match can end in a win, a draw or a loss. The probability of a win is 1/10 and the probability of a draw is 3/20. What is the probability of a loss?” A common wrong answer is 4. / The fraction was turned upside down; 'not E' is what is left when E is taken from the sure event: 1 − P(E).
text: A question: “A match can end in a win, a draw or a loss. The probability of a win is 1/10 and the probability of a draw is 3/20. What is the probability of a loss?” A common wrong answer is 4.
P(win or draw) = 2/20 + 3/20 = 1/4 was turned upside down to get 4, but a probability is never more than 1. 'Not E' is what is left when E is taken from the sure event: 1 − 1/4 = 3/4.
entries.problem: The wrong answer 4 comes from 1 ÷ P(win or draw), but the explanation ('the fraction was turned upside down') does not show this and never says that a probability can't be more than 1.

text: Each step builds on another skill: Find the probability of an event; Simplify fractions. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Find the group you are told about (the girls), then the fraction of that group with the property (in the chess club).
entries.problem: 'Combine quantities within 20' is not the prerequisite a Class 11 conditional-probability skill builds on; it needs fractions/basic probability.

entries.original: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together (A ∩ B is empty). Independent events have P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B). Two events that both can happen cannot be both. / Count n(A), n(B) and n(A ∩ B). If n(A ∩ B) = 0 they are mutually exclusive. Otherwise compare P(A ∩ B) with P(A) × P(B).
text: Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together (A ∩ B is empty). Independent events have P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B). If P(A) and P(B) are both more than 0, the events cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent.
Count n(A), n(B) and n(A ∩ B). If n(A ∩ B) = 0 they are mutually exclusive. Otherwise compare P(A ∩ B) with P(A) × P(B).
entries.problem: 'Two events that both can happen cannot be both' is garbled; the intended fact is that events with non-zero probabilities cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent.

entries.original: Subtracting the smaller number does not change which numbers divide both cards, so the game ends at the largest number that divides both starting numbers: their HCF. / Write the pair after each move in a table. Keep replacing the larger number by the difference until the two numbers are equal.
text: In the game two cards show two numbers; each move replaces the larger number by the larger minus the smaller. Subtracting the smaller number does not change which numbers divide both cards, so the game ends at the largest number that divides both starting numbers: their HCF.
Write the pair after each move in a table. Keep replacing the larger number by the difference until the two numbers are equal.
entries.problem: Refers to 'the game' and 'both cards' without describing the game, and uses HCF without saying how the pair changes.

entries.original: Kaprekar noticed that repeating this routine on four-digit numbers always seems to reach 6174 — a conjecture you can test with your own numbers. Each step must be done exactly.
text: Kaprekar's routine takes a four-digit number (not all digits the same), makes the largest and the smallest numbers from its digits, and subtracts. Kaprekar noticed that repeating this on four-digit numbers always seems to reach 6174, a conjecture you can test with your own numbers. Each step must be done exactly.
entries.problem: Refers to 'this routine' without saying what Kaprekar's routine is.

entries.original: A conjecture is a guess from patterns: every four-digit number (not all digits equal) reaches 6174 by Kaprekar's routine in at most 7 steps; repeated digit sums give the remainder on dividing by 9 (or 9); reversing and adding usually reaches a palindrome. Testing many numbers builds confidence, but only a proof makes it certain. / Carry out the process carefully, writing every number, and count the steps. Check against the conjecture: the answer for Kaprekar is never more than 7; the digit-sum answer is the remainder on dividing by 9.
text: A conjecture is a guess from patterns: every four-digit number (not all digits equal) reaches 6174 by Kaprekar's routine in at most 7 steps; repeated digit sums give the remainder on dividing by 9 (or 9 when the number divides exactly by 9); reversing and adding usually reaches a palindrome. Testing many numbers builds confidence, but only a proof makes it certain.

Carry out the process carefully, writing every number, and count the steps. Check against the conjecture: the answer for Kaprekar is never more than 7; the digit-sum answer is the remainder on dividing by 9 (9 if that remainder is 0).
entries.problem: 'give the remainder on dividing by 9 (or 9)' is garbled; the digit sum is 9, not 0, when the number divides by 9.

entries.original: Every multiple of a is a multiple of b exactly when b divides a (6 → 3 works, 3 → 6 does not: 9). / For n² and n: if a has no square factor, every prime of a must already divide n.
text: 'Every multiple of a is a multiple of b' is true exactly when b divides a. For example, every multiple of 6 is a multiple of 3, but not every multiple of 3 is a multiple of 6: 9 is a counterexample.

For n² and n: if a divides n², does a divide n? It does when no prime appears twice in a (like 6 = 2 × 3), because each prime of a dividing n² must divide n. It can fail otherwise: 4 divides 2² but not 2.
entries.problem: Too compressed to follow: '6 → 3 works, 3 → 6 does not: 9' and 'if a has no square factor, every prime of a must already divide n' are not explained.

entries.original: A question: “For whole numbers n, consider the statement: "If n is a multiple of 4, then n² is a multiple of 4." Which is correct about this statement and its converse?” A common wrong answer is 0. / The converse was assumed to be true exactly when the statement is; a converse swaps the 'if' and 'then' parts and must be checked on its own.
text: A question: “For whole numbers n, consider the statement: "If n is a multiple of 4, then n² is a multiple of 4." Which is correct about this statement and its converse?” A common wrong answer is 'both are true'.

The converse was assumed to be true because the statement is. The converse, 'if n² is a multiple of 4 then n is a multiple of 4', is false: n = 2 gives n² = 4. A converse swaps the 'if' and 'then' parts and must be checked on its own.
entries.problem: The wrong answer is given as '0', which is meaningless for a question asking which statement about truth values is correct.

entries.original: Making the photo 24 cm wide by adding 12 cm on both sides would give 24 cm by 20 cm: the height is no longer the same part of the width, so the picture is stretched or squashed. / Multiplying both sides by 24 ÷ 12 gives 24 cm by 16 cm: the height and the width change in the same ratio, so the shape is kept.
text: A photo is 12 cm wide and 8 cm tall. Making it 24 cm wide by adding 12 cm to both sides would give 24 cm by 20 cm: the height is no longer the same part of the width, so the picture is stretched or squashed.
Multiplying both sides by 24 ÷ 12 = 2 gives 24 cm by 16 cm: the height and the width change in the same ratio, so the shape is kept.
entries.problem: The photo's original size (12 cm by 8 cm) is never stated, so the numbers cannot be followed.

entries.original: Each step says what happens and, after the dash, why.
text: Each step says what happens and, after the dash, why.
Go first and take 3, leaving 12 — 12 is a multiple of 4 (1 + 3 = 4).
Your friend takes 1, 2 or 3; you take 3, 2 or 1 — together you take 4, so 8 are left.
Do the same again: 4 left, then 0 — you take the last match, because your friend always faces a multiple of 4 and can never take all of it.
entries.problem: A 'Worked' example that has no steps: it only says that each step will have a reason.

entries.original: A question: “f: ℝ → [−3, ∞) is given by f(x) = 2x² − 3. Which is true?” A common wrong answer is 3. / A square was assumed never to be onto; the codomain here is [−3, ∞), and every y in it is reached. It is not one-one, since f(−1) = f(1).
text: A question: “f: ℝ → [−3, ∞) is given by f(x) = 2x² − 3. Which is true?” A common wrong answer is 3.
A square was assumed never to be onto; the codomain here is [−3, ∞), and every y in it is reached, so f is onto. It is not one-one, since f(−1) = f(1). So f is onto but not one-one.
entries.problem: 'Which is true?' gives no options, so the wrong answer '3' is meaningless to the learner.

entries.original: A question: “On A = {1, 2, 3}, the relation R = {(1, 1), (1, 3), (3, 1)}. Which statement about R is true?” A common wrong answer is 3. / Reflexive needs (a, a) for EVERY a in A; one missing pair is enough to fail.
text: A question: “On A = {1, 2, 3}, the relation R = {(1, 1), (1, 3), (3, 1)}. Which statement about R is true?” A common wrong answer is 'R is reflexive'.
Reflexive needs (a, a) for EVERY a in A; (2, 2) and (3, 3) are missing, so R is not reflexive. R is symmetric, but not transitive: (3, 1) and (1, 3) are in R but (3, 3) is not.
entries.problem: The wrong answer is given as '3', which means nothing to the learner; the explanation also omits that R is not transitive either.

Sort the data and take the middle value as the median M (for 7 values, the 4th). Add the distances |x − M| and divide by the number of values.
entries.problem: Says 'take the 4th value' and 'divide by 7' as a general method, though no data set of 7 values is given.

entries.original: Find the median of 66, 58, 75, 81, 14, 95. In order they are 14, 58, 66, 75, 81, 95: with 6 numbers there are two middle numbers (66 and 75), and the median is halfway between them. / With an even number of values there are two middle values: take halfway between them.
text: A common mix-up is to give just one of the two middle values. Find the median of 66, 58, 75, 81, 14, 95: in order they are 14, 58, 66, 75, 81, 95, and with 6 numbers there are two middle numbers, 66 and 75.
Giving 66 or 75 is wrong: with an even number of values the median is halfway between the two middle values, (66 + 75) ÷ 2 = 70.5.
entries.problem: Titled as a common mix-up, but it never says what the mix-up is and never gives the median's value.

entries.original: A question: “The clustered bar chart shows how many children of Class 9A and Class 9B walk to school and how many come by bus. If the same data were drawn as a 100% stacked bar chart, which class would have the longer 'walk' part of its bar?” A common wrong answer is 1. / The class with more walkers was chosen. A 100% stacked bar shows each class as a whole (100%), so it compares the share of walkers, not the number.
text: A question: “The clustered bar chart shows how many children of Class 9A and Class 9B walk to school and how many come by bus. If the same data were drawn as a 100% stacked bar chart, which class would have the longer 'walk' part of its bar?” A common wrong answer is the class with more walkers.
That compares numbers of walkers. A 100% stacked bar shows each class as a whole (100%), so it compares the share of walkers, not the number.
entries.problem: The question asks which class (9A or 9B), but the 'common wrong answer' is given as '1', which is not one of the choices.

entries.original: Get the ratio on its own, then find the reference angle α: the acute angle whose ratio is the value without its sign. Sine is positive in quadrants I and II, so the solutions are α and π − α.
text: Get the ratio on its own, then find the reference angle α: the acute angle whose ratio is the value without its sign. Then keep the quadrants where the ratio has the right sign: for example, sine is positive in quadrants I and II, so for sin x = a positive value the solutions are α and π − α.
entries.problem: States the solutions are always α and π − α, which is true only for a positive sine value; cos, tan and negative values use other quadrants.

entries.original: Each observation point gives a right triangle; the two triangles share the height h, and their bases differ by the distance walked. / Let x be the distance from the nearer point. Write h = x tan β and h = (x + d) tan α, set them equal, solve for x, then find h.
text: Each observation point gives a right triangle; the two triangles share the height h, and their bases differ by the distance walked.

Let x be the distance from the nearer point, where the angle of elevation is β, and let α be the angle at the farther point, d further away. Write h = x tan β and h = (x + d) tan α, set them equal, solve for x, then find h.
entries.problem: The angles α and β are used without saying which point each belongs to.

That is why it has a single value. / Find the standard angle whose ratio is the argument, then make sure it lies in the principal range: for a negative argument use −θ (sin⁻¹, tan⁻¹, cosec⁻¹) or π − θ (cos⁻¹, sec⁻¹, cot⁻¹).
text: Each inverse function returns one angle from its principal range: sin⁻¹ in [−π/2, π/2]; tan⁻¹ in (−π/2, π/2); cosec⁻¹ in [−π/2, π/2] without 0; cos⁻¹ in [0, π]; cot⁻¹ in (0, π); sec⁻¹ in [0, π] without π/2. That is why it has a single value.
Find the standard angle whose ratio is the argument, then make sure it lies in the principal range: for a negative argument use −θ (sin⁻¹, tan⁻¹, cosec⁻¹) or π − θ (cos⁻¹, sec⁻¹, cot⁻¹).
entries.problem: The ranges given are wrong: tan⁻¹ is (−π/2, π/2), not the closed interval; cot⁻¹ is (0, π); cosec⁻¹ leaves out 0 and sec⁻¹ leaves out π/2.

entries.original: A question: “What is the domain of cos⁻¹ (the set of real numbers x for which cos⁻¹(x) is defined)?” A common wrong answer is 2. / The principal range of cos⁻¹ was given instead of its domain: the domain is the set of numbers x that cos⁻¹ accepts.
text: A question: “What is the domain of cos⁻¹ (the set of real numbers x for which cos⁻¹(x) is defined)?” A common wrong answer is 2.
The principal range of cos⁻¹, [0, π], was given instead of its domain: the domain is the set of numbers x that cos⁻¹ accepts, [−1, 1].
entries.problem: A domain question with the 'wrong answer 2' makes no sense; the options are missing.

entries.original: A question: “Find the exact value of cos 45° − tan 60°.” A common wrong answer is (3√2 − 2√3)/6. / The values of sin and cos were swapped (and tan taken as cot): for example sin 30° = 1/2 and cos 30° = √3/2.
text: A question: “Find the exact value of cos 45° − tan 60°.” A common wrong answer is (3√2 − 2√3)/6.
entries.problem: The wrong answer comes from taking tan 60° as 1/√3 (cos 45° is unchanged by swapping sin and cos), but the explanation talks about swapping sin/cos with an unrelated 30° example and never gives the correct value.
